ops.title: Automating with Zapier — Apps, AI Actions & SaaS Connections
Why Zapier at all — the dependency argument

ops.markdown:
The class opened on the fair challenge: why learn Zapier when n8n already did everything? The answer was not asserted, it was demonstrated.

**The exhibit.** A real n8n canvas of his own — schedule, GitHub push history, trending repos, filters, README fetch, four LLM chains, merge, email, plus side branches writing files back to GitHub. The class was asked to explain it. Nobody could, end to end, with ten minutes to try.

> "This flow is best understood by who created it."

The canvas is not broken and not badly built. It is unreadable by anyone else, and that turns out to be a property with consequences.

### Wanderline's three complaints

1. **It works, but it is not beginner-friendly** — "this is what keeps their Saturday and Sunday occupied." The people who live with it pay in weekends.
2. **Ownership is limited to one person.** Keep this precise: you *can* export an n8n workflow — three-dot menu gives JSON, or box-select the canvas and copy, because "all these nodes are nothing but configurations." The **artefact** is portable. What is not is that a published workflow on one account is visible and editable only by that account. Running it and owning it are different things.
3. **If that person goes, no one wants to touch it.**

**What the third one costs.** His own 2018 Excel-aggregation script, written by someone who left. `git blame` showed the lines untouched from 2018 until a 2024 migration forced the issue — because "it was vulnerable to breaking down if you make a lot of changes." Six years of nobody touching working code, not because it was wrong but because understanding it cost more than leaving it alone.

A student named it: **creating dependency.**

Note that none of the three complaints is technical. They are about who can read it, who can edit it, and who dares change it. Day 12 asked whether work suits a machine; this asks the question after it — **once built, who can live with it?**

### Zapier's structural answer

**A Zap has exactly one trigger.** n8n lets you put three, four, ten triggers and several independent workflows on one canvas. Zapier does not. One trigger, then actions, top to bottom.

Read that as a declined feature rather than a missing one. The constraint is what buys readability: one entry point and one direction means "what starts this and what happens next" has an answer you can read off the screen. The exhibit had no such answer. The trade is expressiveness for maintainability, and whether it is a good trade is what the comparison returns to.

Side note on knowledge transfer: KT videos plus `.md` files explaining the code, "so you can use that when you're using AI to make code changes." Nobody watches the videos later — but he has had to.

ops.title: Action vs task, and what it costs

ops.markdown:
**The cricket bat.** Swinging a bat in the air is an **action** — the capability exists, the motion happened. Hitting a ball that someone actually bowled is a **task**: "that is what has real tangible effect… you hit the ball and you get runs."

Translated: a *Send message* step sitting in a Zap is an action. The moment it actually sends, that is a task. A Zap that sends an email, then a chat message, then an SMS is **three tasks per run**.

This is the most consequential definition in the lecture, because it is the billing unit. Two things follow immediately:

- **The bill scales with steps × runs**, not with how many Zaps you own. Ten Zaps that never fire cost nothing; one Zap with five steps firing hourly is expensive.
- **A step that runs and achieves nothing still costs you.** Nothing about a wasted task looks different from a useful one on the invoice.

That second point is why Filter is taught as a shield rather than as a gate, and it is the whole of the filter-placement quiz.
